title: Judge Orders DOJ to Halt Threats of Prosecution Against Election Officials, Politico Reports
body:
A federal judge in San Francisco has issued a sweeping injunction that bars the Department of Justice from threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution over how they resolve disputes about voter eligibility. The order, handed down Friday, also prohibits federal officials from demanding that ballots from selected voters be set aside for separate review, a practice the court said undermines established election procedures and could chill the administration of elections nationwide.

The ruling comes after a series of complaints from election administrators in several states who said they were receiving letters and memoranda from the DOJ’s civil rights division that warned of possible criminal liability if they failed to “segregate” ballots cast by individuals whose eligibility was under question. Those directives, the plaintiffs argued, conflicted with state laws and the federal Voting Rights Act, and placed an undue burden on local officials already stretched thin by the aftermath of the 2020 election cycle. In a detailed opinion, the judge found that the DOJ’s actions exceeded its statutory authority and amounted to an impermissible threat of prosecution.

Legal experts note that the decision marks a rare rebuke of the Justice Department’s use of its enforcement powers in the highly politicized arena of election law. “The court is essentially saying that the DOJ cannot weaponize the threat of criminal charges to influence how states conduct their elections,” said Professor Elena Ramirez, a constitutional law scholar at Georgetown University. “While the department has a legitimate role in safeguarding voting rights, it must do so within the bounds of the law, not by coercing local officials into actions that may not be legally required.” The judge’s language underscores this point, emphasizing that the federal government cannot compel states to adopt procedures that are not grounded in statutory or regulatory authority.

The injunction also touches on a broader controversy that has unfolded since the 2020 presidential election, when the DOJ and other federal agencies intensified scrutiny of voting practices in battleground states. Critics argue that the heightened oversight was motivated by partisan concerns, while supporters contend that it was necessary to prevent fraud and ensure election integrity. The court’s order does not address the underlying allegations of voter fraud; rather, it focuses on the manner in which the DOJ communicated its concerns to election officials. By halting the “threat” of prosecution, the ruling seeks to restore a measure of autonomy to local election administrators, allowing them to follow state statutes and established federal guidelines without fear of punitive action.

State officials have welcomed the decision as a reaffirmation of state sovereignty over election administration. California’s Secretary of State, who filed the lawsuit on behalf of several local jurisdictions, called the ruling “a victory for the rule of law and for the countless workers who keep our democracy functioning day after day.” Conversely, the Justice Department has signaled its intent to appeal, arguing that the injunction oversteps judicial authority and hampers the department’s ability to enforce federal voting statutes. In a brief statement, the DOJ’s civil rights division said it will “seek clarification from the appellate courts” and continue to pursue “legitimate enforcement actions” where evidence of violations exists.

The broader implications of the decision could reshape the dynamic between federal oversight and state control of elections, especially as the nation approaches the 2028 presidential contest. If the appellate courts uphold the injunction, the DOJ may need to revise its approach to addressing voter‑eligibility disputes, focusing on collaborative guidance rather than coercive threats. Legal scholars suggest that the case could become a touchstone for future disputes over the balance of power in election administration, potentially prompting Congress to clarify the scope of the Justice Department’s authority in this arena. For now, election officials across the country can proceed with their existing processes, reassured that the specter of federal prosecution will no longer loom over routine decisions about ballot handling.
